title: Trump Announces Phased Tariffs of Up to 200% on Generic Drug Imports
excerpt: The new tariff plan gives generic drugmakers a two-year duty-free window before imposing 100% tariffs from August 2028 and 200% from 2029, rattling Indian pharma stocks.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Generic drug imports to the U.S. will face phased tariffs starting in August 2028.
  • Indian pharma stocks fell, with Nifty Pharma index dropping nearly 2% after the announcement.
  • India supplies 47% of U.S. generic prescriptions, but many generics are priced significantly lower than branded drugs.
  • Several Indian drugmakers have FDA-approved U.S. facilities, aiding potential reshoring efforts.
  • India's reliance on China for APIs poses a long-term risk to its pharmaceutical industry.
Phased Tariffs on Generic Drugs
August 1, 2026
Generic drugs enter U.S. tariff-free period.
August 2028
100% tariff imposed for one year.
August 2029
200% tariff takes effect.

President Donald Trump on Tuesday unveiled a phased tariff plan targeting imported generic medicines, completing a broader strategy to bring nearly every category of pharmaceutical imports under a tariff framework. The move has immediate implications for India, the world's largest supplier of affordable generic drugs to the American market.

In a Truth Social post, Trump wrote that all generic drugs entering the U.S. will face zero tariffs for two years from August 1, 2026. After that, a 100% tariff kicks in from August 2028 for one year, followed by a 200% levy from August 2029 onward.

Indian Markets React Sharply

The announcement sent Indian pharmaceutical stocks tumbling. The Nifty Pharma index fell nearly 2% in early trade on Wednesday, making it the worst-performing sectoral index on the NSE. Aurobindo Pharma dropped 3.48%, Lupin declined 3.46%, and Cipla fell 1.51%. Sun Pharmaceutical Industries edged lower by 0.98%, while Dr. Reddy's Laboratories slipped 1.33%, according to Analytics Insight.

European generic drugmakers were not spared either. Switzerland's Sandoz fell around 3%, while Germany's Fresenius dropped 1.4% and London-listed Hikma Pharmaceuticals lost 0.8%, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Why India's Generic Drugs May Remain Competitive

Despite the steep proposed tariffs, India's generic medicines could retain significant competitiveness. According to the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), many Indian generics sell at seven to ten times below the price of branded alternatives. Even after a 100% tariff, many products could remain cheaper than branded drugs — meaning the additional cost would likely be absorbed by U.S. healthcare providers, insurers, and patients rather than eliminating Indian exports outright.

"This is done in order to RESHORE Generic Pharmaceutical Production into America, with a penalty to those Companies that decide not to build Plant and Equipment within the stated period of time given to them."

— Donald Trump, via Truth Social

India's pharmaceutical exports to the U.S. totaled $9.7 billion in 2025, representing 37.7% of its total pharma exports of $25.8 billion globally. Indian companies supply 47% of all generic prescriptions dispensed in the United States, though their share of the value of U.S. generic imports is estimated at only 30% because generics sell at such low prices, GTRI data shows.

Reshoring Challenges and Industry Response

Several of India's leading pharmaceutical companies already have FDA-approved manufacturing operations in the U.S. Sun Pharma, Zydus Lifesciences, Lupin, Aurobindo Pharma, Cipla, and Dr. Reddy's Laboratories all operate facilities there. Cipla is expanding capacity at plants in Massachusetts and New York. Dr. Reddy's has said it can increase U.S. production if commercially viable.

But analysts caution that moving large-scale generic drug manufacturing to the U.S. is far from straightforward. Generic medicines operate on thin profit margins and rely heavily on global supply chains, particularly for active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), a significant share of which comes from India and China.

Analysts at J.P. Morgan wrote in a note that Trump's proposal might be a starting point for negotiations with generics manufacturers, and that the tariff plan seems unlikely to be implemented in its current form given it could result in cost increases for U.S. patients, according to the Wall Street Journal.

The Diaspora Dimension

For the Indian diaspora in the U.S., the proposed tariffs could mean higher prescription drug costs down the line. Generic medicines account for more than 90% of prescriptions filled in the country, according to the FDA. Any disruption to the supply chain — or price increases passed through to consumers — would affect millions of patients, including a substantial Indian American community that relies on affordable generics.

A Bigger Challenge Lurks

GTRI founder Ajay Srivastava points to a longer-term risk that may outweigh U.S. tariffs: India's dependence on China for APIs. About 70% of chemical-based APIs used by Indian drugmakers and nearly 90% of biologic inputs come from China. If China curbs API exports while expanding its own finished drug shipments, India's pharmaceutical industry could face severe supply-chain disruptions.

Srivastava argues India should prioritize rebuilding its API manufacturing base while diversifying exports to Europe, Latin America, Africa, and Asia. The two-year window before tariffs take effect also leaves considerable room for the policy to be revised, postponed, or overturned through legal or political developments.

For now, the pharmaceutical industry is watching and waiting. The phased timeline offers breathing room, but the direction of travel is clear: Washington wants drug manufacturing on American soil, and the world's generic medicine suppliers have two years to decide how to respond.
